questions.q: Machine G stretches its input by $3\times$ and Machine F stretches its input by $2\times$. Feeding an input through G then F, how much does a small change get stretched?
questions.explain: The Chain Rule multiplies the rates: $3 \times 2 = 6$. Adding them ($5$) is the most common mistake.
Outer $f(g) = \sin(g)$ gives $\cos(g)$, inner $g(x) = x^2$ gives $2x$. Multiply and plug the inner layer back in: $\cos(x^2) \cdot 2x$. $\cos(x^2)$ forgets the inner slope.

questions.q: In the lab's Power preset, $g(x) = 0.5x^2 - 2$ and $f(g) = 0.2g^2$. What is $\frac{df}{dx}$ at $x = 3$?
questions.explain: $g(3) = 2.5$, $g'(3) = 3$, $f'(g) = 0.4g = 1$. So $\frac{df}{dx} = f'(g) \cdot g'(x) = 1 \times 3 = 3$. $1$ is only the outer slope.

questions.q: How does backpropagation use the Chain Rule in a network $\text{Loss}(\text{Layer3}(\text{Layer2}(\text{Layer1}(w))))$?
options: It multiplies the local slopes of each layer along the path from the Loss back to the weight (summing over paths when there are several)
It adds the layers' outputs together
It only uses the slope of the last layer
It differentiates each layer with respect to the Loss independently and averages them
questions.explain: Backpropagation is the Chain Rule applied systematically backwards: local derivatives are multiplied along each path, and contributions from different paths are added.
